entry.title: [推荐] Rethinking (De)growth: the politics of compost
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Jessica Croteau

Moving beyond economic analyses of degrowth, growth and consumption are reframed through decomposition as a vital process through which life, value, and politics are continually re-composed. Against dominant imaginaries that cast decay as waste or ruination, this article turns to composting and carrion ecologies to articulate decomposition as a generative undoing and a mode of transformation that binds waste to worth. Drawing on multispecies examples from vultures in India to the Baltimore Compost Collective, the article situates decomposition as both material process and political metaphor to enact a revaluation of growth, decay, and consumption that unsettles capitalist logics of extraction and accumulation. entry.title: [推荐] The subject of intelligence: AI as existential risk and the government of the human and the future
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Caio Simoneti

This article analyses discourses on artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of existential risk studies. AI appears as a key theme in existential risk circles, not only as a source of risk, but also as a resource for risk prevention and as the enabler of a glorious future for humanity. However, what is it about AI that brings together utopian and dystopian imaginaries? Why is a discourse on AI so tied to questions regarding the human, and what forms of humanity does it produce? What forms of governing does it enable? This article argues that the concept of ‘intelligence’ is fundamental regarding both how AI is construed as an existential risk, as well as how humanity is conceptualised as that which needs to be protected. entry.title: [推荐] Is religion a problem for intersectional theory? Muslim women, feminism, and varieties of patriarchy
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (3.0)

Karolin I. M. Tuncel、Tobias Müller

Intersectional theory has been criticised for neglecting religion and for being unable to account for religion’s social complexities. This contribution interrogates this critique by disaggregating different relationships of Muslim women to secular and religious varieties of patriarchy. We argue that what demarcates the challenges of intersectional analysis are the political contestations not around religion, but around women’s pro-patriarchal agency. We do so by discussing intersectional theory’s analytical usefulness and limitations in conceptualising the experiences of Muslim women. entry.content:
Political Theory · Vol. 54 No. 5 699-723 · 必读 (7.0)

Rita Koganzon

Political theorists have long focused their understanding of democratic education on the institution of the school, particularly the public school, to the exclusion of broader visions of education beyond schooling. But as criticisms of schooling from outside the academy mount, it becomes imperative to examine the origins of American educational thought to determine whether opposition to schooling has an older historical source. This essay locates the roots of school skepticism in an alternative American educational tradition beginning with Benjamin Franklin that drew on Locke’s pedagogical arguments to devalue institutional schooling in favor of self-education. entry.title: [推荐] The Utilitarian Classical Liberalism of Ludwig von Mises and Its Libertarian Misreception
entry.content:
Political Theory · Vol. 54 No. 5 749-772 · 推荐 (3.0)

Jonathan Cole

This article examines Ludwig von Mises’s utilitarianism in the context of his liberal social theory. It contends that he sought to reorient classical liberalism away from natural law theory and refound it in utilitarianism. This significant shift distinguishes and differentiates Misesian liberalism from the classical liberal tradition with which Mises consciously identified it, as well as later Rothbardian libertarianism, which, while identifying with the Misesian tradition, reverted to a natural law philosophy that produced irreconcilable differences with Misesian liberalism over the legitimacy of the state.

entry.content:
Political Theory · Vol. 54 No. 5 724-748 · 推荐 (3.0)

Nicholas A. Anderson

The fact that Toward Perpetual Peace is presented as a satirical peace treaty is a detail that has been largely overlooked in the literature. This article argues that when one reads Toward Perpetual Peace with its formal presentation in mind, what emerges is a work of philosophical literature that acts politically through its rhetorical form. The article shows how Kant—through what is here called his rhetoric of hope—offers a political education to two kinds of readers: the many, who are susceptible to a “despotic” moralism, and the elite, who embrace the principles of a selfish despotism. entry.content:
Political Theory · Vol. 54 No. 5 653-676 · 推荐 (3.0)

Clare Woodford、Michelle Bentley

This article offers a feminist reworking of Adriana Cavarero’s conceptualization of horrorism as a form of extreme violence that targets and dehumanizes its victims through dismemberment and an ontological assault on human uniqueness. While Cavarero’s intervention is motivated by a commitment to resisting patriarchal logics of war and reorienting political thought toward care, we argue that her framework depends on an overly fixed opposition between the monstrous perpetrator and the defenseless victim, exemplified in her reading of Medusa in contrast with the Christian Madonna. The binary risks reproducing the very logics of exclusion and moral absolutism it seeks to disrupt. entry.title: [推荐] "A Place Dedicated to Openness of Mind": Why Academic Freedom Protects "Distasteful" Extramural Speech
entry.content:
Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 682-706 · 推荐 (3.0)

Nicholas Tampio

: This article explains why academic freedom protects "distasteful" extramural speech, including social media posts outside of a scholar's area of expertise. Initially, I explain why using the First Amendment to protect academic freedom jeopardizes the latter. Next, I describe how German philosophers and American pragmatists expounded academic freedom to protect a community of strong-willed scholars. Then, I note that the AAUP has backed away from defending the Enlightenment-Romantic conception of the good supporting academic freedom. Finally, I argue that academic freedom should protect both Plato and Diogenes, polite and confrontational scholars.

entry.title: [推荐] Portraits of Absence: Listening to the Kidnapped Posters
entry.content:
Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 707-740 · 推荐 (3.0)

Alyson Cole

: Images are sites and key media of struggle. This essay shows how such conflicts play out—both via form and through use—and why that matters for the study of politics. Analyzing the visual politics of #KidnappedFromIsrael provides a critical yet undertheorized perspective on the hostilities that erupted in American cities over Israel/Palestine after October 7. Through this case study I endeavor to make four contributions: 1. define a visual genre, "portraits of absence," which publicizes suffering in distinct ways; 2. extend critical phenomenologists' conceptualization of "perceptual habits" to the not-Other; 3. explicate and trouble binaries undergirding empathic visual practices; 4. reassess the relationship between virtual and physical sites of political contestation.

Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 741-774 · 推荐 (3.0)

Jeanne Morefield

: This article investigates the role of trafficking narratives in early-twentieth-century liberal internationalist world-making. Focusing on the League of Nations' anti-trafficking campaign, I demonstrate how these efforts contributed to such liberal worldmaking through what I call under worldmaking. I use Edward Said's notion of imaginative geography to explore the League's fixation with the relationship between global civility and global criminality, treating it as an adaptation of imperialism's Manichaean geopolitics for the new internationalist age. I focus on the Traffic in Women and Children's committee's process of knowledge production, arguing that the parallel trafficking underworld they worked so hard to capture also shared figurative entailments with antisemitic conspiracy theories. entry.title: [推荐] The Collapse of Shame: Corruption as Genre in a Post-Truth Age. Toward a Cultural Theory of Public Impunity
entry.content:
Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 775-786 · 推荐 (3.0)

Jacqueline Fendt

: This essay argues that corruption today functions not as scandal but as genre—performed, aestheticized, and infrastructurally sustained. In an era where shame collapses and impropriety becomes spectacle, corruption no longer hides: it signals power. Impunity now takes shape as public demonstration, staged and circulated as proof of sovereignty. Corruption, shame, and impunity form a new circuitry: corruption provides the recognizable form, shame recedes into spectacle, and impunity choreographs authority through performance. To understand democratic erosion today, we must analyze and expose this choreography—not only legally, but culturally, emotionally, and structurally.

entry.title: [推荐] Complaints about the Weather: Eco-Neurosis in Jonathan Safran Foer and Jenny Offill
entry.content:
Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 787-813 · 推荐 (3.0)

Hans Demeyer

: This essay identifies eco-neurosis as an affective response to the environmental crisis. Aware that their lives contribute to this crisis, the eco-neurotic polices their consumption and lifestyle patterns, yet simultaneously remains attached to the good life promise under capitalism: a double bind that causes compulsive thoughts and feelings. If such eco-neurosis causes an affective displacement, this essay proposes the complaint as a genre that expresses such neurosis and offers the promise of renewed belonging. A reading of eco-neurosis in Jonathan Safran Foer's We Are the Weather (2019) and Jenny Offill's Weather (2020) shows how the complaint however preserves the double bind.

This article discusses how seascapes became an issue of datafication in the British East India Company’s campaign toward global economic hegemony in the later 18th century. entry.content:
Constellations · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (10.7)

E. Lawrence Bradford

In the 1920s and 1930s, Walter Benjamin and Theodor W. Adorno both sought to develop a notion of Darstellung —of philosophical presentation or representation—that could provide an alternative to the classically idealist tendency to subsume objects under abstract concepts. Benjamin's influence on Adorno is therefore often narrativized through the latter's early work, in which Adorno appears as Benjamin's “disciple” in the 1930s before later developing an independent philosophical voice. I seek to complicate this narrative through an investigation of the term “constellation,” which appears prominently in Benjamin's work before being repurposed by Adorno. Theory, Culture & Society · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (5.0)

Javier Lezaun

This article interprets the geological sequestration of carbon dioxide as an opportunity to re-imagine the appropriability of nature and its resources. While the extraction of hydrocarbons was historically supported by radical innovations in the definition of legitimate ownership – most notably the relentlessly expansive interpretation of the ‘rule of capture’ in the United States – the need to inject billions of metric tonnes of CO₂ into the lithosphere to achieve any measure of climate stabilization has not generated any meaningful change in juridical reasoning. Legal and economic constructions of geologically sequestered carbon are for the most part parasitic on the measures of value and the modes of appropriation that legitimize fossil fuel mining.
